html:
In 1873 Russian troops took Khiva, and the treaty that made the Khanate of Khiva a Russian protectorate ended the slave trade there. Khiva, in the oasis of Khwarazm south of the Aral Sea, held one of the last big slave markets in Asia.

For centuries Turkmen and Kazakh raiders had seized Persians from Khurasan and Russians from the Caspian shore and the frontier, and sold them in Khiva and Bukhara to work the irrigated fields and serve in households. Persians were by far the most numerous, and in the early 1800s the slaves numbered in the tens of thousands. Freeing Russian captives was Russia's stated reason for its failed campaign against Khiva in 1839 and again in 1873.

Khan Muhammad Rahim II freed the slaves in his land as the Russians closed in, and many Persians made their way home. Bukhara agreed to a similar ban the same year. Slavery lingered quietly for a time, but the great markets closed. It was part of the Russian conquest of Central Asia that brought the Uzbek khanates under the tsar.
